subtopic_detail: Facial nerve palsy complicating acute otitis media versus idiopathic Bell palsy in a child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on call. A 5 year old girl is brought in by her father because the right side of her face has been drooping since he woke her this morning. She has had a sore right ear for four days and has been hot and off her food.

She cannot wrinkle her forehead or close her right eye, and the right corner of her mouth does not move when she cries. The right tympanic membrane is bulging, red and immobile on pneumatic otoscopy. There are no vesicles in the ear canal or on the pinna, and the remaining cranial nerve and limb examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Complete right upper and lower facial weakness, bulging immobile right tympanic membrane, no mastoid tenderness or postauricular swelling
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); C-reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone for five days together with lubricating eye drops
options.rationale: Corticosteroid is the treatment for idiopathic facial palsy, but a bulging infected drum on the same side identifies an intratemporal cause, and steroid without drainage and antibiotics leaves the infection untreated (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media).

options.text: Oral amoxicillin for five days with review by her general practitioner in 48 hours
options.rationale: Oral amoxicillin is right for uncomplicated acute otitis media, but any intratemporal complication moves the child to intravenous therapy and inpatient care rather than community review (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Admit for intravenous antibiotics with urgent ear nose and throat review for myringotomy
options.rationale: Facial weakness with an acutely infected middle ear is a complicated otitis media, and treatment is intravenous antibiotic cover plus drainage of the middle ear to decompress the nerve in its canal (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral aciclovir and prednisolone with an urgent outpatient audiology appointment
options.rationale: Antiviral plus steroid targets herpes zoster oticus, whose near pair feature is vesicles in the canal or on the pinna with severe otalgia rather than a bulging purulent drum (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media).

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is reserved for slowly progressive weakness, other cranial nerve signs or suspected intracranial extension, and delaying antibiotics for a scan in a febrile child with an obvious middle ear source risks further spread (Source: RCH CPG: Acute Otitis Media).

explanation.summary: Facial nerve palsy in a child is only idiopathic once a middle ear cause has been excluded, because the nerve runs through the middle ear in a bony canal that is dehiscent in a proportion of children. Suppuration under pressure produces a lower motor neurone weakness that resolves when the middle ear is drained and the organism treated. The other intratemporal complications to look for at the same time are acute mastoiditis, labyrinthitis and sigmoid sinus thrombosis. Missing the ear and treating as idiopathic palsy with steroid alone risks permanent weakness and intracranial spread.
key_points: Examine both tympanic membranes in every child with facial weakness before labelling it idiopathic
Complicated acute otitis media means admission, intravenous antibiotics and ear nose and throat involvement
Myringotomy both decompresses the middle ear and yields fluid for culture
Vesicles in the canal or on the pinna point instead to herpes zoster oticus
Eye protection is still needed while the eye will not close, whatever the cause
explanation.pearls: A lower motor neurone facial palsy that spares no forehead movement plus a bulging drum is complicated otitis media until proven otherwise, and the drainage should happen on the day of presentation rather than after a trial of oral antibiotics.

subtopic_detail: Persistent bilateral otitis media with effusion and the threshold for ventilation tube referral
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 4 year old boy whose parents have been coming back about his hearing since the autumn. They say he turns the television up, does not answer when called from another room, and that his kindergarten teacher has raised that other children are hard to understand him.

You first documented dull immobile drums with visible fluid levels at a visit four months ago and again eight weeks ago, and today both drums look the same. He has had no ear pain, discharge or fever in that time. A formal audiogram today shows a bilateral conductive loss averaging 35 dB with flat tympanograms.

data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes dull and retracted with an air fluid level, no perforation or discharge, normal facial movements
data_table.Investigations: Pure tone audiometry bilateral conductive loss averaging 35 dB; type B flat tympanogram bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for consideration of ventilation tubes
options.rationale: Effusion documented beyond three months with a bilateral loss of this size and a clear effect on speech and learning meets the referral threshold, and tubes are the intervention that restores hearing while the eustachian tube matures (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

options.text: Prescribe a two week course of oral amoxicillin and reassess the drums afterwards
options.rationale: Antibiotics clear effusion only transiently and confer no benefit on hearing at three months, and there is no acute infection here to treat (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

options.text: Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray and review the audiogram in three months
options.rationale: Intranasal steroid has no demonstrated effect on effusion clearance or hearing, and a further three months of waiting adds to an already documented four month history (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

options.text: Reassure the parents and review again in three months with a repeat audiogram
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is correct for the first three months because most effusions resolve, but that window has already passed and the loss is affecting speech (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the temporal bones before any referral
options.rationale: Temporal bone imaging is for suspected cholesteatoma or a bony complication, neither of which is suggested by intact retracted drums with fluid behind them (Source: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

explanation.summary: Otitis media with effusion is fluid in the middle ear without the features of acute infection, and it is extremely common in preschool children after upper respiratory illness. The great majority resolve spontaneously within three months, which is why the first response is documented watchful waiting with an audiogram rather than treatment. Referral is driven by the combination of persistence beyond three months, the size of the hearing loss and a demonstrable effect on speech, language or schooling, not by the appearance of the drum alone. Left untreated in that group the child accumulates months of degraded auditory input during the years when speech sounds are being laid down.
key_points: Three months of documented persistence is the usual trigger to move from watching to referring
A type B flat tympanogram supports effusion but the audiogram quantifies the disability
Antibiotics, antihistamines, decongestants and intranasal steroid do not change outcomes
Speech, language and behaviour concerns lower the threshold for referral
Autoinflation devices are a reasonable adjunct in older cooperative children
explanation.pearls: A bilateral conductive loss of 25 to 30 dB is roughly the volume difference between normal speech and a whisper, which is why a child with persistent effusion at that level appears inattentive rather than deaf.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Otitis Media with Effusion

subtopic_detail: Rapidly worsening atopic eczema with punched out erosions and the decision to treat as viral superinfection
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department. A 2 year old girl with moderate atopic eczema has become much worse over 36 hours. Her mother says the rash on her face and neck now looks like small round sores that all seem the same size, that they are weeping clear fluid, and that her daughter screams when anything touches them.

She has been febrile at home and has refused to drink since last night. Her eczema is usually controlled with a moderate potency topical corticosteroid and she started that again two days ago without improvement. The lesions extend onto the right upper eyelid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9
data_table.Examination: Clustered uniform 2 to 3 mm shallow erosions with haemorrhagic crusting over face and neck, lesions on the right upper eyelid, no purulent discharge or honey coloured crust
data_table.Investigations: Viral swab of a deroofed lesion sent for polymerase chain reaction; white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase to a potent topical corticosteroid and arrange dermatology review this week
options.rationale: Escalating topical steroid onto an untreated cutaneous herpes infection allows it to spread, and this is the classic anti-pattern that turns a treatable superinfection into a disseminated one (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema).

options.text: Start oral cefalexin and continue the current topical corticosteroid at home
options.rationale: Oral cefalexin covers staphylococcal impetiginisation, whose distinguishing feature is golden crusting and pustules rather than uniform punched out erosions that are exquisitely painful (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Apply wet dressings with bleach baths and review in the ambulatory clinic tomorrow
options.rationale: Wet dressings and dilute bleach baths reduce bacterial load in chronic eczema but do nothing for viral replication, and outpatient review defers treatment in a child who is febrile and not drinking (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema).

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin and admit for observation overnight
options.rationale: Immunoglobulin has no role in cutaneous viral superinfection of eczema and would delay the specific antiviral that changes the course (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema).

options.text: Admit for intravenous aciclovir with same day ophthalmology review of the eye
options.rationale: Painful monomorphic punched out erosions spreading rapidly across eczematous skin in a febrile child who is not drinking warrants intravenous antiviral therapy, and periocular involvement needs slit lamp assessment on the same day (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Children with atopic eczema have a defective skin barrier and reduced cutaneous antimicrobial defence, so herpes simplex acquired from a cold sore in a carer can spread across affected skin rather than staying localised. The give away is that the lesions are all the same age and shape, are painful rather than itchy, and appear on eczematous rather than intact skin. Bacterial superinfection often coexists, which is why antistaphylococcal cover is usually added, but the antiviral is the treatment that alters the trajectory. Involvement near the eye is a separate emergency because corneal disease can scar, and dissemination to the liver and brain is the feared systemic outcome in an unwell infant.
key_points: Uniform punched out erosions on eczematous skin that hurt rather than itch suggest herpetic superinfection
Fever and poor oral intake move treatment from oral to intravenous antiviral therapy
Do not escalate topical corticosteroid onto suspected herpetic eczema
Periocular lesions require same day ophthalmology assessment
Send a deroofed lesion swab for viral polymerase chain reaction but treat before the result
explanation.pearls: Aciclovir gives the greatest benefit when started within the first 48 hours of the eruption, so treat on the clinical pattern of monomorphic painful erosions and do not wait for the polymerase chain reaction result.

subtopic_detail: First line treatment choice in primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis at school age
stem:
You are the paediatric outpatient registrar seeing a 7 year old boy referred for bedwetting. His mother says he has never had a run of dry nights, that it happens most nights, and that he sleeps so heavily he does not wake when it happens. He is dry during the day with no urgency, wetting or straining, and he opens his bowels to a soft stool daily.

He is otherwise well, is growing along the 50th centile and is doing well at school. His mother has already reduced evening drinks and started lifting him at 11 pm without any change. He is upset about missing a school camp in six months.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable faecal loading, normal external genitalia, normal lower limb neurology and normal lumbosacral spine
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for glucose, protein, blood, nitrites and leucocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe oxybutynin at night and review his bladder diary in eight weeks
options.rationale: Anticholinergic therapy targets overactive bladder, whose distinguishing feature is daytime urgency and wetting, and this boy has no daytime symptoms at all (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Start an enuresis alarm with review of the record after four to six weeks
options.rationale: An alarm is the first line treatment for primary monosymptomatic enuresis in a motivated child of this age because it produces the highest sustained dry rate after treatment stops (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Prescribe oral desmopressin nightly and review his response after four weeks
options.rationale: Desmopressin works quickly and is valuable for short term cover such as a camp or a sleepover, but relapse on stopping is the rule so it is not the first choice for durable dryness (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Begin a macrogol disimpaction regimen and reassess the wetting in six weeks
options.rationale: Treating occult constipation is the correct first move when there is loading or infrequent hard stools, but he passes a soft stool daily and has no palpable loading (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Arrange a renal tract ultrasound and refer to a paediatric urology clinic
options.rationale: Imaging and urology referral are for daytime symptoms, abnormal stream, recurrent infection or neurological signs, and a normal examination with clear urinalysis does not warrant them (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

explanation.summary: Bedwetting is called monosymptomatic when there are no daytime storage or voiding symptoms, and primary when the child has never had a six month dry spell. Before any treatment the two reversible contributors to exclude are constipation and urinary tract infection, because treating either can resolve the wetting on its own. Alarm therapy conditions the child to wake or inhibit voiding and has the best relapse free outcome, but it demands household commitment for six to eight weeks and does not suit every family. Desmopressin has a role as rapid short term cover and as a fallback when an alarm fails or is impractical.
key_points: Exclude constipation and urinary infection before labelling enuresis primary and monosymptomatic
Daytime urgency, wetting or straining shifts the diagnosis away from simple nocturnal enuresis
Alarm therapy has the highest sustained dry rate after treatment ceases
Desmopressin is the practical option for camps and sleepovers
Fluid restriction and lifting are not effective as sole measures
explanation.pearls: Continue an enuresis alarm for at least two weeks beyond fourteen consecutive dry nights before stopping, since ceasing at the first run of dry nights is the commonest cause of early relapse.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing positional head shape deformity from premature suture fusion in an infant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar at a 5 month immunisation visit. The mother says the back of her son's head has looked flattened on one side since about six weeks of age and that it has not changed since she started giving him more time on his tummy.

Looking down on the vertex from above, the right occiput is flattened, the right ear sits forward of the left, and the right forehead is more prominent than the left. The anterior fontanelle is soft and open and the sutures feel mobile with no palpable ridge. He turns his head fully to both sides against gentle resistance and his head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening with ipsilateral anterior displacement of the ear and forehead, open mobile sutures, full passive and active neck rotation both ways
data_table.Investigations: Head circumference on the 50th centile at 6 weeks, 3 months and today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the skull with three dimensional reconstruction
options.rationale: Skull computed tomography carries a radiation dose and is reserved for cases where fusion is suspected clinically, which requires a palpable ridge or a head shape that does not fit a positional pattern (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).

options.text: Refer urgently to a craniofacial surgical unit for consideration of vault surgery
options.rationale: Craniofacial referral is for premature suture fusion, in which the ear on the flattened side is displaced backwards and the head shape is trapezoid rather than a parallelogram (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).

options.text: Fit a custom moulding helmet now and review the head shape again in three months
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is an option only for severe deformity that has not responded to repositioning, and trial evidence shows no advantage over conservative measures for mild to moderate cases (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).

options.text: Continue repositioning and tummy time and review the head shape in three months
options.rationale: A parallelogram head with the ear pushed forward on the flattened side, mobile sutures and a normal head circumference is positional, and it remodels with repositioning as the child begins to sit and roll independently (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for stretches to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle this week
options.rationale: Physiotherapy is indicated when a shortened sternocleidomastoid restricts rotation and drives the positional preference, but rotation is full and symmetrical here (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly).

explanation.summary: Positional head shape deformity became far more common after infants began sleeping on their backs, and it is benign and self correcting in the large majority. The single most useful bedside discriminator is the position of the ear on the flattened side, because gravity pushes the whole hemicranium forwards in a positional deformity while a fused suture tethers it backwards. Premature fusion also restricts growth across the affected suture, so head circumference often deviates from its centile and a bony ridge becomes palpable. Because congenital muscular torticollis both causes and is maintained by the positional preference, neck rotation must be assessed at the same visit.
key_points: Positional deformity gives a parallelogram vertex with the ear and forehead displaced forwards
Premature suture fusion gives a trapezoid vertex with the ear displaced backwards and a palpable ridge
Serial head circumference that stays on its centile argues against fusion
Always test neck rotation because torticollis maintains the positional preference
Helmets are reserved for severe deformity after repositioning has failed
explanation.pearls: Look at the vertex from directly above the infant rather than from the front, since the forward displacement of the ear that separates positional deformity from lambdoid fusion is visible only on that view.

subtopic_detail: Radiographic discrimination of an ingested disc battery from a coin and the resulting urgency
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 2 year old boy was found next to an opened remote control about 90 minutes ago and his father thinks he swallowed something from it. He gagged once, cried briefly and has been drinking water since without difficulty.

He is alert with no drooling, stridor or respiratory distress. An anteroposterior chest radiograph shows a 20 mm rounded radiodense object at the level of the thoracic inlet with a narrow rim of lower density around its circumference, and the lateral film shows a step off in its profile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118, blood pressure 94/56, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Handling secretions normally, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and non tender
data_table.Investigations: Anteroposterior and lateral chest radiographs as described; no free air under the diaphragm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange immediate endoscopic removal in theatre and give honey while awaiting transfer
options.rationale: The peripheral rim on the frontal film and the step off on the lateral identify a disc battery rather than a coin, which causes hydroxide mediated mucosal injury within two hours, so removal is immediate and honey buffers the alkali in the interval (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

options.text: Repeat the radiograph in six hours and remove endoscopically only if it has not passed
options.rationale: Serial films to document passage is the approach for a coin lodged in the oesophagus of an asymptomatic child, but delay of even a few hours with a battery allows full thickness burn (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

options.text: Discharge with advice to check the stools and return if he develops any new symptoms
options.rationale: Expectant management applies once a small blunt object has cleared the oesophagus into the stomach, and this object is still at the thoracic inlet where injury occurs fastest (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

options.text: Give oral activated charcoal and admit for observation with hourly nursing review
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind an intact battery and adds aspiration risk before an anaesthetic, and observation substitutes monitoring for the removal that the injury mechanism demands (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

options.text: Induce vomiting with a gastric irritant and repeat the radiograph after the attempt
options.rationale: Induced emesis is contraindicated for any ingested foreign body because it risks aspiration and drags the corrosive surface back across already injured mucosa (Source: RCH CPG: Button Battery Ingestion).

explanation.summary: A lithium disc battery lodged in the oesophagus generates hydroxide ions at its negative pole and produces liquefactive necrosis within two hours, long before the child becomes symptomatic. The radiographic signs that separate it from a coin are a double rim or halo on the frontal projection and a step off in profile on the lateral, so both views are mandatory whenever the history mentions a remote control, hearing aid, toy or greeting card. Because the mechanism is chemical rather than obstructive, a well child who is drinking normally provides no reassurance at all. The late complications, which can present days to weeks after removal, include tracheo oesophageal fistula, oesophageal stricture and fatal aorto oesophageal fistula.
key_points: Always obtain frontal and lateral films because the halo and step off signs need both
Injury begins within two hours, so a well child is not a reason to wait
Honey is given while awaiting removal in a child over 12 months who can swallow safely
Do not induce vomiting and do not give charcoal
Follow up matters because stricture and fistula present after removal
explanation.pearls: Give 10 mL of honey every 10 minutes up to six doses while transferring a child over 12 months to theatre, but withhold it entirely if there is drooling or suspected perforation.

subtopic_detail: Observation period and disposition after a brief unwitnessed submersion in a well child
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a district hospital. A 3 year old girl was pulled from a backyard pool about four hours ago after her grandmother noticed her missing for less than a minute. She was face down but came up coughing immediately and cried at once. No rescue breaths or compressions were given.

She coughed intermittently for about ten minutes in the car and has been playing in the waiting room since. Her chest is clear and she has maintained normal saturations on room air throughout four hours of continuous monitoring in the department. Her parents want to know whether she needs to stay in overnight in case her lungs fill up later.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Alert and playful, chest clear with equal air entry, no cough on exertion, no accessory muscle use
data_table.Investigations: Continuous pulse oximetry over four hours with no desaturation; no chest radiograph performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Obtain a chest radiograph and admit if any interstitial change is seen on the film
options.rationale: A radiograph in an asymptomatic child yields findings that do not predict deterioration and generates admissions on radiological rather than clinical grounds (Source: RCH CPG: Drowning).

options.text: Admit overnight for continuous oximetry because deterioration can occur up to 24 hours later
options.rationale: The idea of a symptom free child deteriorating many hours afterwards is not supported by outcome data, and every child who worsened did so within the first hours after immersion (Source: RCH CPG: Drowning).

options.text: Discharge home with written advice and address pool fencing before she leaves
options.rationale: A child who is asymptomatic with normal saturations after four to six hours of observation may go home, and the encounter is the moment to act on the four sided isolation fencing that prevents the next event (Source: RCH CPG: Drowning; Royal Life Saving Australia).

options.text: Start prophylactic amoxicillin clavulanate and review in the short stay unit tomorrow
options.rationale: Prophylactic antibiotics after immersion in clean water do not prevent pneumonia and select resistant organisms, and they are considered only for grossly contaminated water with established infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone and observe for a further four hours
options.rationale: Corticosteroid has no role in aspiration related lung injury and exposes the child to hyperglycaemia and immunosuppression without benefit (Source: RCH CPG: Drowning).

explanation.summary: Drowning injury is driven by the volume and duration of aspiration, and a child who never needed rescue breathing and who has normal respiratory effort and saturations has almost certainly aspirated a trivial volume. The terms secondary and dry drowning have been formally retired because the phenomenon they described, a well child collapsing many hours later, does not appear in prospective series. What does happen is that a child with persistent cough, crackles, hypoxia or altered conscious state at presentation progresses over the following hours, which is why the decision point is the clinical state at four to six hours rather than the story of the immersion. In Australia the majority of toddler drownings occur in domestic swimming pools with a fencing defect, so the safety conversation is a core part of the presentation.
key_points: Four to six hours of observation is sufficient for an asymptomatic child after immersion
Cough, crackles, hypoxia or drowsiness at any point during observation mandates admission
Chest radiography and blood tests are not indicated in the asymptomatic child
Prophylactic antibiotics and corticosteroids have no role
Toddler pool drowning in Australia is overwhelmingly associated with a fencing or gate failure
explanation.pearls: Any child who required rescue breaths at the poolside is admitted regardless of how well they look on arrival, since assisted ventilation at the scene is the single strongest predictor of subsequent respiratory deterioration.

subtopic_detail: First aid and antivenom decision after a spider bite where pressure immobilisation is contraindicated
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a Sydney hospital at 9 pm. A 6 year old boy was bitten on the back of the right calf 40 minutes ago while pulling a bike out from under a garden bench. His mother killed the spider and has brought it in; it is small, dark and shiny with a red stripe on the upper abdomen.

He is distressed and says the pain has spread up his thigh and is getting worse, and he is sweating heavily over the bitten leg. No first aid was applied. There is a small red mark on the calf with local sweating around it, and his abdomen is soft with no guarding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Examination: Punctum on the right calf with localised piloerection and sweating, pain radiating to the groin, normal conscious state, no fasciculation or muscle spasm
data_table.Investigations: Point of care testing not indicated; no coagulation studies performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Apply a pressure immobilisation bandage to the whole leg and splint it, then observe
options.rationale: Pressure immobilisation is used for snake and funnel web bites where the venom is life threatening and systemic, but here it concentrates venom locally and markedly worsens the pain (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline 9.4.7).

options.text: Give intravenous antivenom immediately and admit to the high dependency unit overnight
options.rationale: Antivenom for this genus is considered only after simple measures fail because its benefit over placebo is contested, and it is given intravenously without high dependency care in an otherwise stable child (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Apply an ice pack and give oral analgesia, then reassess the pain in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Cold and simple analgesia are the first measures for this bite, and reassessment determines whether opioid or antivenom is needed, since pressure immobilisation would make the pain worse (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council Guideline 9.4.7; Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Take blood for coagulation studies and creatine kinase before giving any analgesia
options.rationale: Coagulopathy and rhabdomyolysis screening belongs to snakebite assessment, and this venom produces neither, so testing delays the analgesia that is the actual treatment (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

options.text: Infiltrate the bite site with local anaesthetic and discharge once the pain has settled
options.rationale: Local infiltration does not relieve pain that is already radiating proximally through a systemic mechanism, and discharge before a period of reassessment misses progressive envenomation (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology).

explanation.summary: Australian first aid for bites and stings splits sharply on whether the venom is rapidly life threatening. Snake, funnel web spider, blue ringed octopus and cone snail envenomation all receive pressure immobilisation bandaging to slow lymphatic spread, while red back spider, other spiders, jellyfish, bee and scorpion stings do not, because trapping the venom locally intensifies the pain without any survival benefit. Red back envenomation causes local sweating and piloerection at the site with pain that radiates centrally and can persist for days, but it is not associated with coagulopathy, myotoxicity or death in the modern era. Antivenom remains available and is considered for pain uncontrolled by opioid analgesia or for systemic features, though a randomised Australian trial found its benefit over placebo hard to demonstrate.
key_points: Pressure immobilisation is for snake, funnel web, blue ringed octopus and cone snail only
Local sweating and piloerection at the bite with radiating pain is the red back pattern
Ice and oral analgesia first, escalating to opioid before considering antivenom
No coagulation or muscle enzyme testing is required for this envenomation
Funnel web bites instead cause fasciculation, salivation and autonomic storm and are a true emergency
explanation.pearls: Localised sweating confined to the skin around the bite is close to specific for red back envenomation and is the finding that distinguishes it from the generalised sweating and fasciculation of a funnel web bite.

subtopic_detail: Sleep study before adenotonsillectomy when the airway phenotype is atypical for tonsillar hypertrophy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic. A 4 year old boy with trisomy 21 is referred because he snores every night, and his mother describes pauses in his breathing that end with a gasp, and says he sleeps with his neck extended and is exhausted during the day.

He has a repaired atrioventricular septal defect with normal ventricular function on echocardiography six months ago. His tonsils are small and sit well within the tonsillar pillars, and his body mass index is on the 95th centile. He has a small midface, a relatively large tongue and mild generalised hypotonia. The referring letter asks whether he should simply have his tonsils and adenoids removed.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils graded 1 of 4 bilaterally, midface hypoplasia, relative macroglossia, generalised hypotonia, no chest wall deformity
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram six months ago with repaired defect and normal ventricular function; overnight oximetry not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial an intranasal corticosteroid for six weeks and reassess the snoring afterwards
options.rationale: Intranasal steroid can help mild obstruction driven by adenoidal tissue, but witnessed apnoeas with daytime somnolence in a high risk child require characterisation rather than an empirical trial (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

options.text: Arrange a laboratory polysomnogram before deciding on any surgical intervention
options.rationale: Small tonsils, midface hypoplasia, macroglossia and hypotonia mean the obstruction is multilevel rather than tonsillar, so severity and the site of obstruction must be measured before an operation that may not resolve it (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea; Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Refer for adenotonsillectomy on the strength of the witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness
options.rationale: Proceeding on history alone is reasonable when large tonsils explain the obstruction, but residual disease after surgery is common in this syndrome and the tonsils here are grade 1 (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

options.text: Start continuous positive airway pressure at home and review his symptoms in three months
options.rationale: Positive airway pressure is a legitimate treatment in this group, but pressure titration and mask fitting depend on the sleep study that has not yet been done (Source: Australasian Sleep Association).

options.text: Repeat the echocardiogram to look for pulmonary hypertension before any further assessment
options.rationale: Pulmonary hypertension is the feared consequence of untreated obstruction and warrants an echocardiogram in due course, but it grades the complication rather than establishing the diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive Sleep Apnoea).

explanation.summary: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the usual cause of obstructive sleep apnoea in otherwise healthy preschool children, and in that setting a convincing history with large tonsils justifies surgery without a sleep study. Trisomy 21 breaks that shortcut, because obstruction arises from midface and mandibular hypoplasia, relative macroglossia, pharyngeal hypotonia and central obesity as well as from lymphoid tissue. Around half of these children have significant residual disease after adenotonsillectomy, so the operation is planned against measured severity and a known site of obstruction rather than offered blind. Australian practice is to screen this group with polysomnography around four years of age regardless of parental report, because habitual snoring is under recognised and untreated disease causes pulmonary hypertension, neurocognitive impairment and behavioural difficulty.
key_points: Tonsil size that does not match symptom severity signals multilevel obstruction
Trisomy 21 carries a high rate of residual apnoea after adenotonsillectomy
Polysomnography quantifies severity and separates obstructive from central events
Overnight oximetry can confirm severe disease but a normal result does not exclude it
Untreated paediatric obstructive sleep apnoea causes pulmonary hypertension and neurocognitive harm
explanation.pearls: Australian sleep guidance recommends a polysomnogram for every child with trisomy 21 by about four years of age even when the parents report no snoring, because parental report has poor sensitivity in this group.

subtopic_detail: Adolescent hip pathology presenting as referred knee pain with a normal knee examination
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 12 year old boy has had a dull ache in the front of his left thigh and knee for six weeks, worse after football, with no injury. He has been seen twice for the same complaint and given a knee brace and simple analgesia without improvement. He walked in today but says the leg feels like it is giving way.

His knee has full painless range with no effusion, no joint line tenderness and negative ligament testing. When you flex the left hip the leg rolls into external rotation, and internal rotation of that hip is limited to 5 degrees with pain at the extreme. His weight is above the 97th centile. He is afebrile and has had no weight loss or night pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 122/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Normal knee examination, obligate external rotation of the left hip on passive flexion, internal rotation limited to 5 degrees, no groin swelling or erythema
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 7.1 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an outpatient knee magnetic resonance scan and continue the brace meanwhile
options.rationale: Knee imaging pursues the site of the pain rather than its source, and a full painless knee range with no effusion places the lesion at the hip (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Aspirate the left hip under ultrasound guidance after taking blood cultures
options.rationale: Aspiration is for suspected joint sepsis, which presents over days with fever and raised inflammatory markers rather than six weeks of activity related ache with normal bloods (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Prescribe regular ibuprofen with physiotherapy for the hip and review in four weeks
options.rationale: Loading a hip in this state risks converting a stable slip into an unstable one, and the resulting avascular necrosis rate rises many fold (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Make him non weight bearing and obtain frog lateral pelvic views with orthopaedic referral
options.rationale: Obligate external rotation on hip flexion with restricted internal rotation is the classic sign, the displacement is often visible only on the lateral projection, and unloading the hip before surgery prevents progression to an unstable slip (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

options.text: Request a technetium bone scan of both lower limbs to localise the source of the pain
options.rationale: Bone scanning is used when plain films are normal and the site is genuinely unclear, whereas here the examination localises the hip and a two view radiograph will answer the question far faster (Source: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

explanation.summary: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is the commonest hip disorder of adolescence and is repeatedly missed because roughly a quarter of children present with knee or distal thigh pain alone, referred along the obturator nerve. The diagnosis is protected by two habits: examining the hip in every child with knee pain, and ordering a frog lateral as well as an anteroposterior view, since early posterior displacement of the epiphysis may be invisible on the frontal film. Risk is concentrated in overweight peripubertal children, and endocrine causes such as hypothyroidism and growth hormone deficiency should be considered in a child who is young, thin or has bilateral slips. The clinical distinction that determines prognosis is stable versus unstable, defined by whether the child can weight bear, because avascular necrosis follows an unstable slip in a substantial minority.
key_points: Examine the hip in every adolescent presenting with knee pain
Obligate external rotation on passive hip flexion is the most reliable bedside sign
Order anteroposterior and frog lateral pelvic views, not a knee series
Make the child non weight bearing as soon as the diagnosis is suspected
Consider endocrine screening in an atypically young, thin or bilateral case
explanation.pearls: Progression from a stable to an unstable slip raises the risk of avascular necrosis from under 5 per cent to nearly 50 per cent, which is why the child goes onto a trolley the moment the diagnosis is suspected rather than walking to radiology.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
BMJ Best Practice: Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
